After the plaintiff was handcuffed, the officers proceeded with him to the unit 4 dining hall. Here Stefanus Mwandingi indicated that he was indeed in contact with the plaintiff.  The plaintiff then informed the witness that he was using the phone of a certain Richard Katjitenga in unit 5.  He further informed the witness that he was in pain and the witness gave instructions that the plaintiff was to be taken to the clinic.  The plaintiff was at no time assaulted or kicked in the presence of the witness.

Tomas Shaanika

[14]	Tomas Shaanika holds the rank of Senior Chief Correctional Supervisor stationed at the Windhoek Correctional Facility and is also the Officer in Charge in unit 6 in the said facility.  On 2 May 2022 at about 16h00 a cell and body search was conducted at unit 4 and unit 6 of the facility.  The search was conducted in terms of s 38(1) of the Correctional Service Act, 9 of 2012 which allows a correctional officer to conduct a search of any offender who is within the correctional facility in the prescribed manner and circumstances.

[15]	Upon arrival at unit 6, the witness had the master key that opened all the gates of the cells in that unit.  He saw the plaintiff coming from the side of the bed section going to the bathroom.  He instructed all the offenders to stand next to their beds and informed them that a search would be conducted but the plaintiff remained in the bathroom.  After the offenders were searched, the witness instructed them to move outside the cell.  Ian Jones was also outside the cell and not inside the cell as he alluded in his testimony.  The witness was not inside the bathroom when the plaintiff was handcuffed and can therefore not say what happened there.  He however did not observe any injuries or blood on the plaintiff when he came outside the cell.  He was further not present when the plaintiff was taken to the dining hall.  He saw that the plaintiff was cuffed normally with his hands behind his back.

[16]	He further testified that the plaintiff used to complain to him to be taken to the hospital but he does not know the nature of the illness the plaintiff had.

Josef Moses

[17]	The witness is an Enrolled Nurse, employed by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security, and stationed at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  On 2 May 2022 at about 17h45 he was at home on standby duty when he was called to the facility to see a patient, the plaintiff.  Upon his arrival at the clinic he found some officers who informed him that the plaintiff injured himself on the floor.  He proceeded and performed a physical examination on him.  He examined the plaintiff.  He further observed that the plaintiff had a history of a broken tooth, which he believes to be from an old injury.  He further proceeded to ask the plaintiff what his complaints were and the plaintiff indicated that he had injured himself on the floor.  He did not tell the witness how and what happened.  

[18]	According to the witness’ observation the plaintiff’s front tooth (number 11) had a loose part which was cracked from the inside, this is called an inner tooth fracture.  He observed that only the fractured part of the tooth was loose and the rest of the tooth was still intact.  He further indicated that in his expertise there should have been some bleeding in the mouth and some swelling if the fracture was recent and occurred on 2 May 2022.  He did however not observe any indication that suggested that the plaintiff fractured his tooth that day.  If he further injured himself on the floor, in the experience of the witness, he would have experienced an outer tooth fracture as opposed to an inner tooth fracture.

[19]	The plaintiff informed him that he was in pain and he administered a pain injection.  He also referred him to the dental clinic at the Katutura Hospital.  He was taken to the Katutura Hospital on 3 May 2022 where after he opted to see a private dental practitioner for further management.

Simeon Shangala

[20]	The third defendant is employed by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration, Safety and Security:  Office of the Commissioner-General and holds the rank of Senior Chief Correctional Officer.  He is stationed at unit 3 at the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  On Monday, 2 May 2022 at 16h00, a cell and body search was conducted at unit 4 and 6 of the Windhoek Correctional Facility.  This was upon instructions from the Head of Security due to the unlawful escape from custody by an inmate Simon Kambindu.  During their search they found inmate Simon Kambundi with an illegal cell phone.  The call log indicated communication with a certain “Dix” whom was identified by the said Simon Kambindu at the plaintiff.  	

[21]	They proceeded to unit 6 and the witness saw the plaintiff moving from the bed section to the bathroom.  All the offenders were instructed to stand next to their beds and informed of the search.  The Plaintiff however remained in the bathroom but he was not washing his clothes as he testified.  The officers conducted a body search on the offenders and a sim card was found on the plaintiff.  The offenders were then instructed to stand outside the cell against the wall.  Only the plaintiff and the officers remained in the cell.  Ian Jones was not inside the cell.  The witness denies slapping the plaintiff with an open hand, neither that he kicked him in the stomach or head with booted feet.  When they found the sim card on him, they wanted to handcuff him and take him for further questioning.  The plaintiff however resisted and informed them that “whoever touches my body will see, I am having a lawyer”.  The officers then used minimal force to force the plaintiff to the ground and placed handcuffs on him.  He was not handcuffed in the nr.8 position.

[22]	The plaintiff did not break his tooth during this process, neither was he bleeding or had a swollen mouth and neither was he assaulted.  After he was handcuffed, the plaintiff was taken to the dining hall of unit 4 where Stefanus Mwandingi confirmed that he was communicating with the plaintiff on a cell phone.  The plaintiff then requested to speak to Senior Superintendent Sakaria where he informed him that the cell phone he used was with Richard Katjitenja.  

Exhibits
[23]	During the trial, the following documentary evidence was tendered:
(a) “Exhibit A” - Medical records of Katutura hospital and Oyetweni Dental Practice.
(b) “Exhibit B” - Affidavit in terms of s 212 (4) (a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 (J88 report) 
(c) “Exhibit C” – Plaintiff’s health passport

Arguments by the parties

[24]	The Plaintiff’s version before the court was that he was assaulted by the correctional officers, slapped by the third Defendant (witness number 4), kicked with booted feet, and stomped on his head and in the process broke his tooth. Plaintiff further testified he was bleeding and his mouth was swollen, his version was corroborated by the three witnesses who came across as credible witnesses. The Defendant’s evidence is that the officers never assaulted the Plaintiff, they testified that minimum force as provided for by the Correctional Service Act and its Regulations was used to restrain and handcuff the Plaintiff as he was aggressive. All witnesses failed to put on record how the Plaintiff was aggressive. The Defendant’s further evidence was that the Plaintiff was restrained by approximately 8 officers. It was also the Defendant’s evidence that the Plaintiff was taken to the facility clinic after complaining of pain. The court is faced with two mutually destructive versions.

[25]	It was submitted that the explanation by the plaintiff that he broke this tooth that day, and he was bleeding and swollen, is the most probable version before the court. This version was corroborated by three witnesses, and the evidence that the plaintiff was bleeding and swollen was never refuted or challenged by the defendants legal practitioner during cross-examination. The evidence adduced by the plaintiff and his witnesses regarding the bleeding was left unchallenged in cross-examination.

[26]	It was further argued that the plaintiff testified that he was handcuffed and attacked by approximately 10 officers. This version was confirmed by the defendants witnesses that about 8 officers who were present. The defendants case was that they needed to use so many officers, because the plaintiff was aggressive; however, when put to the witnesses how aggressive the plaintiff was, they failed to demonstrate to the court. Witness Ipinge Sakaria was very evasive when the question of aggression was put to him, and as such, his evidence must be approached with caution. The only reasonable inference that can be drawn is that in this scuffle, comparing the ratio of the officers to the offender, the plaintiff lost his tooth in the process. The version that reflects what truly transpired on 2 May 2022 is that of the plaintiff.

[27]	It was argued on behalf of the defendants that it is a fact that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his body by the defendants and that violation, if proved, I wrongful and unlawful. Once that is proved, the onus shifts to the defendants to find some sort of legal justification, such as self-defence.  In the current instance, this was not done and the only evidence before court suggests that the third defendant and fellow officers only used minimum force, as allowed for by legislation and regulations, to restrain the plaintiff and to subsequently cuff him.  There is no evidence that he was kicked with booted feet all over his body and head.

[28]	The plaintiff, during his evidence did not focus on any emotional and psychological shock, his claim is thus not substantiated. Rather, the plaintiff focused on the alleged assault and past and future medical expenses.

The legal considerations

[29]	In Harold Schmidt t/a Prestige Home Innovations v Heita it was held that: 

	‘The correct approach would be for the court to apply its mind not only to the merits and demerits of the two mutually destructive versions but also their probabilities and it is only after so applying its mind that the court would be justified in reaching the conclusion as to which opinion to accept and which to reject’

[30]	The court in the case of Von Wielligh v Shaumbwako adopted the reasoning when faced with disparate versions, as follows: 

	‘The plaintiff can only succeed if he satisfies the court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected. In deciding whether that evidence is true or not the Court will weigh up and test the plaintiff’s allegations against the general probabilities. The estimate of the credibility of a witness will therefore be inextricably bound up with the consideration of the probabilities of the case and, if the balance of probabilities favour the plaintiff then the Court will accept his version as being probably true.’

[31]	The principle of mutually destructive versions was also dealt with in the case of Manja v Government of the Republic of Namibia, and the court held that 

	‘[35] In National Employers’ General Insurance v Jagers, Eksteen AJP discussed the approach to mutually destructive evidence and stated the following: ‘In a civil case … where the onus rests on the plaintiff as in the present case, and where there are two mutually destructive stories, he can only succeed if he satisfies the Court on a preponderance of probabilities that his version is true and accurate and therefore acceptable, and that the other version advanced by the defendant is therefore false or mistaken and falls to be rejected.’

[32]	The court in the matter of Namdeb (Pty) Ltd v Gaseb remarked the following regarding failure to challenge the version of the opposing witness: 
	
	‘It is trite law that a party who calls a witness is entitled to assume that such a witness’s evidence has been accepted as correct if it has not been challenged in cross-examination. In Small v Smith 1954 (3) SA 434 (S.W.A) at 438E-G the following was said in respect of this aspect: “It is, in my opinion, elementary and standard practice for a party to put to each opposing witness so much of his own case or defence as concerns that witness and if need be to inform him, if he has not been given notice thereof, that other witnesses will contradict him, so as to give him fair warning and an opportunity of explaining the contradiction and defending his own character. It is grossly unfair and improper to let a witness’s evidence go unchallenged in crossexamination and afterwards argue that he must be disbelieved. Once a witness’s evidence on a point in dispute has been deliberately left unchallenged in cross-examination and particularly by a legal practitioner, the party calling that witness is normally entitled to assume in the absence of a notice to the contrary that the witness’s testimony is accepted as correct. . . . unless the testimony is so manifestly absurd, fantastic or of so romancing a character that no reasonable person can attach any credence to it whatsoever.” ’

[33]	In the case of Kolela v Minister of Home Affairs, Safety and Security, the facts of which are similar to the case before court, the plaintiff was assaulted by correctional officers and sought damages in the amount of N$50 000. The court stated that in cases of assault, the plaintiff bears the onus to prove that there was a violation of his or her bodily integrity by the defendants and that violation, if proved, is prima facie unlawful. Once the infringement is proved, the onus shifts to the defendant, to show some legal justification.

Discussion and findings

[34]	The court is tasked to determine which version presented to court is more believable. In the case of Stellenbosch Farmers Winery Group Ltd and Another v Martell et Cie and Others the court held that, to come to a conclusion on the disputed issues, a court must consider and make findings on (a) the credibility of the various factual witnesses, (b) their reliability, and (c) the probabilities.  In the current matter both parties presented multiple witnesses and when the court evaluates their credibility, the court must find that the credibility of all the witnesses cannot be faulted.  During cross examination of these witnesses, no glaring credibility issues were pointed out.  Regarding the reliability of the witnesses the versions presented on behalf of the plaintiff and the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants, the court finds that generally the witnesses were all reliable.  However when the probabilities of the evidence presented is reviewed, the court finds that the evidence presented by the defendant is in the opinion of the court, more probable.  In making this finding, the court is also sensitive that it will impact on the reliability and credibility findings made earlier.

[35]	The court further accepts that there was some form of assault on the body of the plaintiff but that assault was limited to necessary force as authorized in terms of Regulation 194 of the Namibian Correctional Service Regulations.  From the evidence presented on behalf of the defendants it seems that the plaintiff became aggressive whilst the officers were conducting a search which was also authorized by the Correctional Service Act, 9 of 2012 and the above mentioned regulations.  Based on the evidence presented by Josef Moses it is further found that the type of fracture that the tooth of the plaintiff suffered is one not related to an assault as it was an inner tooth fracture.  The evidence further shows that the plaintiff complained about his teeth on previous occasions.  The J88 further recorded no additional injuries except for a red spot in his eye and a complaint about a sensitive wrist.  There was no evidence specifically lead regarding how the eye came to have a red spot, including medical evidence to explain the type and possible cause of such a spot.  The court thus concludes that the tender wrist of the plaintiff was most probably caused by being handcuffed, and that such handcuffing occurred when the plaintiff was restrained. 	

[36]	The plaintiff also testified that he only spent about N$5000 for the replacement of his tooth, and thus, the defendants submit that damages of N$500,000 for medical expenses is exorbitant. He also failed to call the medical doctors who attended to him to corroborate his evidence. Furthermore, the plaintiff was unable to quantify the amount he claims for countemelia and trauma as per his particulars of claim. His claim for countemelia is unsubstantiated and thus should not be entertained by this Honourable Court. 

[37]	In the result, I make the following order:

1.	The claim of the plaintiff is dismissed with costs.

Reasons for order:

NARIB AJ:

[1]	The court is seized with two applications to amend. Both applications concern amendment of the pleas, - the first one, under case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00017 is by the third parties, to amend the plea to the third-party notice filed by the defendant, - and the second one, under case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00138 is by the defendant to further amend the amended plea to the plaintiff’s particulars of claim. Only the plaintiff opposes the applications.

[2]	The amendments sought seek to raise similar issues and the objections thereto to are in some material respects, also similar. Therefore, both applications were heard together on 17 June 2025, and it is convenient that both be disposed of in a single judgement. I shall proceed to do so.

[3]	The notice of intention to amend on behalf of the third parties was filed on 18 October 2024 and the one on behalf of the defendant was filed on 8 January 2025. The pleadings in the application brought by the third parties closed on 27 February 2025, whereas in the application brought by the defendant, such pleadings closed on 12 March 2025.

[4]	Both applications were initially set down for 16 May 2025, but could not be heard on that day, and the hearing was moved to 17 May 2025, for me to hear the matters, which I did, and upon which I reserved judgment, to be delivered on 8 July 2025.

[5]	I set out the above chronology, just to show that even an application to amend can delay a matter for more than six months and that care must be taken when amendments are initiated, and objections are taken to such amendments. In this matter, in view of the position I take, regarding the amendments, the plaintiff who amongst others, objects to the amendments on the basis that it is brought late in the proceedings and will delay the matter by reopening of the pleadings, is responsible for the further delay in the ultimate finalisation of the proceedings. In my view the amendments should have been conceded or agreed to because the objections taken, in each case, are without merit.

[6]	The amendment sought by the third parties, as I have said above, relates to the plea to the third-party notice which was filed by the defendants. In addition to correcting some typographical errors, the amendment seeks to introduce two additional defences, one aimed at impugning the power, authority, or ability of the defendant to bind the Joint Venture between the defendant and the third parties to the contract entered into between the defendant and the plaintiff, with the additional assertion that the said contract was in any event objectively impossible to perform for a miner at the place from which the copper ore had to be mined, as stipulated in the contract, being Outani Mine and was for this reason concluded as a result of a mistake, misunderstanding or iustus error, and the second seeking to challenge whether there was consensus between the defendant and the plaintiff regarding the quality of the copper ore which had to be delivered in terms of the said contract.

[7]	The allegations relating to the mistake, misunderstanding or iustus error pertain to the quality of the copper that could be obtained from Outani Mine, for delivery to the plaintiff. The agreement describes the commodity as raw copper with the origin as per certificate of origin to be Namibia, the fineness to be ore, and purity to be tested between five percent and 25 percent with the average of 15 percent copper concentrate. Monthly production as per the agreement had to be ‘5000MT’ per month with the average of plus or minus five percent and sizes had to be ‘19mm’.

[8]	The third parties assert as per the intended amendment that it was objectively impossible for any miner in Namibia to produce copper ore of the purity stipulated in the agreement and that the scenario and the facts on which such an agreement is based is so unlikely that the purported conclusion of the agreement cannot be explained other than that it was based on iustus error, vitiating consensus. Either both the plaintiff and the defendant were mistakenly of the view that it was possible to perform in terms of the agreement, but had they known the true position, they would not have concluded the agreement (thus, they were operating under a common mistake), or there was a unilateral mistake by one or both of them (in the case of both, the mistake would be mutual), the inference sought to be drawn being that the mistake, in either case, must have been caused by culpable conduct or statements of the other party.

[9]	The evidence to support the notion that it was impossible to produce the quality and quantity of the copper ore stipulated in the agreement is set out in various witness statements of the witnesses to be called by the defendant and the third parties, including the expert summary of Dr Harwood and Dr Dixon. It was submitted on behalf of the plaintiff that such evidence would have been objected to as being in conflict with the defendant’s pleadings.

[10]	The plaintiff objects to the proposed amendments by the third parties on the bases that the proposed amendments are sought belatedly, at the advanced stage of the proceedings without an explanation under oath for such lateness. The plaintiff maintains further that the proposed amendments constitute a substantial change of front which will require the plaintiff to revisit the matter from the pleadings stage as well as to amplify its witness statements, expert evidence and discovery. The third basis of the objection is that the evidence is not foreshadowed to support the plea in its intended amended form and lastly that the third parties have not acknowledged liability for costs. Since the objections are similar to those raised against the proposed amendment on behalf of the defendant, I propose to deal with both sets of objections at once, herein below. 

[11]	It is common cause that the defendant was jolted into action after the amendments sought to be made on behalf of the third parties were filed and the defendant’s proposed amendments are modelled on those of the third parties. The defendant, in the first instance seeks to introduce an amendment for the proper construction to be placed on the provisions of the agreement dealing with the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. The amendment seeks to state that the purity the copper ore would achieve would be between five percent and 25 percent, alternatively an average of 15 percent copper concentrate, once upgraded to copper ore concentrate and that this could be achieved from raw copper ore with the content of about two percent in the ore. 

[12]	In the event of the above not being sustained, and in the alternative, the proposal sought rectification of the agreement, to reflect the above position, but such an attempt at rectification was abandoned and nothing more needs to be said about it.

[13]	The next amendment sought, seeks to introduce a further alternative defence (in the event of the defendant failing to have the defence based on the plea as amended in the first instance sustained), that the agreement as it stands is vitiated by lack of consensus regarding the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff and that such dissensus was caused by a common fundamental mistake that such a quality of ore existed at the Outani Mine and could be delivered, whereas raw copper ore of such quality does not exist at that mine or anywhere else in Namibia and cannot be delivered.

[14]	The final amendment sought to be introduced is that the agreement is unenforceable for being initially impossible (from the inception) to perform, because the quality of copper ore contended by the plaintiff to be what was agreed, cannot be found at the Outani Mine or anywhere else in Namibia.

[15]	Once again the plaintiff objects to the proposed amendments on the bases that they are sought belatedly, at the advance stage of the proceedings after discovery has already been made, witness statements and expert evidence have been filed, and without an explanation under oath why the amendment is sought so late in the proceedings. 

[16]	The objection is also on the bases that the amendment sought will introduce a change of front at a very late stage of the proceedings, which will require the pleadings, witness statements and discovery to be revisited and that no evidence is foreshadowed that will support the defendant’s plea as amended, as per the proposal. It is also said that the amendment will introduce a version which is mutually exclusive to the defences already contained in the defendant’s plea. In this regard, the plaintiff refers to para 6 of the defendant’s plea as it stands, where the defendant admits the written terms of the agreement. According to the plaintiff, the proposed amendment seeks to contradict that admission and will require contradictory evidence, which is impermissible.

[17]	Finally, the objection is also based on failure to tender costs or failure to acknowledge liability for costs.

[18]	For the assertion that an explanation under oath was required due to the belated nature of the amendment sought, the suggestion appears to be that the notice of intention to amend should have been accompanied by an affidavit explaining why the amendment is sought at such a late stage. This objection was taken before the applications to amend, supported by founding affidavits, were filed and the plaintiff persisted in those objection in argument, despite such affidavits having been filed. The argument is not so much that the explanation so provided is inadequate, but that no explanation is provided for the lateness. 

[19]	Both in the objections and the affidavits resisting the amendments, reliance was placed on the decision in Municipal Council of Windhoek v Pioneerspark Dam Investment CC for the proposition that late amendments are subject to greater scrutiny than before because of their deleterious effect upon the administration of justice and that although it is not a prerequisite for an application under rule 52(4) to be accompanied by an affidavit for simple and formal applications, the application for more substantial amendments such as withdrawing an admission or a substantial change of front would need to be done on affidavit.

[20]	I do not understand the above judgment to require that the notice of intention to amend, in terms of rule 52(1) must be accompanied by an affidavit, where the amendment sought is substantial. The judgment refers to rule 52(4) which makes it plain that the affidavit (and thus the explanation under oath) is required at the stage when a party applies to court for an amendment, after an objection is noted against its notice of intention to amend.

[21]	In the present case, both proponents for amendment filed affidavits explaining why amendments are sought at this late stage. The third parties did not initially retain senior counsel, but when the plaintiff, on 29 July 2024 amended its claim by essentially almost doubling the amount claimed from N$52 057 078,89 to N$88 942 503,90, a need was identified to retain senior counsel. The senior counsel so retained studied the record and realised that a defence along the lines of the proposed amendment should be raised and advised accordingly.

[22]	As for the defendant, when the proposed amendment was filed on behalf of the third parties, it was realised that a similar defence should be taken by the defendant. The requirement in the contract relating to the quality of the copper ore to be delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff was already in dispute, as per the existing plea. I refer to paras four and six of the amended particulars of claim and paras two, four, six and nine of the defendant’s plea, as it stands.

[23]	Thus, the intended amendments, in my view, seek to amplify the existing dispute rather than to constitute a complete change of front, and the delay in filing the amendments was explained. I, accordingly, do not agree that there was no explanation under oath for the late amendment and that the proposed amendment by the defendant constitutes a complete change of front or that the third parties seek to introduce completely new defences to the claim. I reject all such bases for the opposition to the proposed amendments.

[24]	As for the objection that the amendment does not raise a triable issue, I also do not agree with the submissions on behalf of the plaintiff. The third parties’ approach in this regard is clearly founded on the record of the documents as they are in the matter, including what is said in the respective witness statements of the parties. If indeed it is established at the trial, - matter which I am not required to decide at this stage, - that performance in terms of the agreement was impossible from the inception because the raw ore quality stipulated in the agreement is impossible to obtain in Namibia - (as asserted on behalf of the third parties and the defendant), - this may well vitiate the agreement. That is a triable issue, for impossibility of performance, in some instances, excuses performance. There is already a version from an expert witnesses, Dr Dixon and Dr Hawood, that this is indeed the case.

[25]	I do not find the version sought to be raised by the third parties to be mere speculation. Even though they are not parties to the agreement, the bases for lack of consensus in initio, which they seek to raise, are from proper inferences to be drawn from what is contained in the agreement, coupled with the evidence of witnesses as contained in the witness statements, that such quality of copper ore cannot be mined in Namibia, except, perhaps, at the Tsumeb Mine. This may result in the court holding that the contract was impossible to perform from the inception. 

[26]	If both the plaintiff and the defendant believed at the time that such quality of ore could be mined at the Outani Mine, and both were mistaken, they were operating under a common mistake in regard to the subject matter of the agreement. This will be the case if the evidence of Dr Dixon holds sway with the court, except, perhaps in the instance that the court finds that the ore could be obtained from the Tsumeb Mine. The agreement indicates that the ore had to be picked up at the ‘Mine site’ but does not seem to define the ‘Mine site’. This and the implications it has for the parties will have to be cleared up by evidence, but my view remains that these are triable issues.

[27]	I also do not see anything mutually exclusive or destructive in the version now sought to be put up by the defendant and what is contained in para 6 of the existing plea. What is clear to me is that the plaintiff and the defendant are in dispute as to the proper construction to be placed on the terms of the agreement describing the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. That construction will be given by the trial court after hearing evidence and in so far as the plaintiff’s counsel urged me, to at this stage provide an interpretation of that part of the agreement, I decline such an invitation.

[28]	I do so because in the matter of Total Namibia (Pty) Ltd v OBM Engineering and Petroleum Distrubutors CC the Supreme Court, in providing an exposition of the new approach to interpretation, held that the context in which a document is drafted is relevant to its construction in all circumstances and that meaning of words is, to a significant extent, determined by the context in which they are uttered. The Supreme Court went on to hold that 

	‘[23] Again this approach seems to comport with our understanding of the construction of meaning, that context is an important determinant of meaning. It also makes plain that interpretation is 'essentially one unitary exercise' in which both text and context, and in the case of the construction of contracts, at least, the knowledge that the contracting parties had at the time the contract was concluded, are relevant to construing the contract. In accepting that the distinction between 'background circumstances' and 'surrounding circumstances' should be abandoned, courts should remember that the construction of a contract remains, as Harms JA emphasised in the E KPMG case, 'a matter of law, and not of fact, and accordingly, interpretation is a matter for the court and not for witnesses'.

Reliance on the broader context will thus not only be resorted to when the meaning of the words viewed in a narrow manner appears ambiguous. [30]	The objection relating to costs occasioned by the amendment was taken, perhaps without proper application of the mind to the rules applicable to amendments. Rule 52(8) provides that a party giving notice of amendment is, unless the court otherwise orders, liable to pay the costs thereby occasioned to any other party. The plaintiff does not point to any direction to the contrary or why it is of the view that it will otherwise not be entitled to such costs.

[31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. The costs of the application to amend stand on a different footing. They are to be capped in terms of rule 32(11), unless otherwise ordered.

[32]	I also agree with the submission on behalf of all the parties that the court may grant an amendment at any stage of the proceedings, before judgment and also that amendments of pleadings should be allowed in order to obtain a proper ventilation of the dispute between the parties so that justice may be done.

[33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable. In my view, the amendments sought in the present matter should have been agreed to so as to facilitate progress in the proceedings, which have now been delayed for a period of more than six months. I can however not say that the opposition was unreasonable, considering the stage in the proceedings at which the amendments were sought.

[35]	Even though the pleadings, as sought to be amended, involve complex questions of law, the law relating to amendments is trite and I did not have to traverse new terrain. The costs occasioned by the application to amend should be capped in terms of rule 32(11) and should be granted in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with the general rule that such costs are borne by a party who seeks an indulgence.

[36]	Both the third parties and the defendant indicated, during argument, that they are not liable jointly and severally for costs and that each one should cover only a portion of the costs arising from the opposed application for amendment. I agree. The plaintiff’s costs relating to the hearing of the application for amendment, including the costs relating to heads of argument thereanent should be borne on a 50-50 basis by the third parties on the one hand and the defendant on the other. 

[37]	The costs relating to the pleadings in the respective applications for amendment are separate, because the applications were filed separately, under different interlocutory case numbers. Therefore, the defendant and the third parties must bear such costs, severally. However, the overall costs to be recovered, by the plaintiff must not exceed the cap in terms rule 32(11), in either case.

[38]	The costs in terms of rule 52(8) stand on a different footing and must be borne respectively by the third parties and the defendant.

Rule 52(8) provides that a party giving notice of amendment is, unless the court otherwise orders, liable to pay the costs thereby occasioned to any other party. The plaintiff does not point to any direction to the contrary or why it is of the view that it will otherwise not be entitled to such costs.

[31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. The costs of the application to amend stand on a different footing. They are to be capped in terms of rule 32(11), unless otherwise ordered.

[32]	I also agree with the submission on behalf of all the parties that the court may grant an amendment at any stage of the proceedings, before judgment and also that amendments of pleadings should be allowed in order to obtain a proper ventilation of the dispute between the parties so that justice may be done.

[33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable. In my view, the amendments sought in the present matter should have been agreed to so as to facilitate progress in the proceedings, which have now been delayed for a period of more than six months. I can however not say that the opposition was unreasonable, considering the stage in the proceedings at which the amendments were sought.

[35]	Even though the pleadings, as sought to be amended, involve complex questions of law, the law relating to amendments is trite and I did not have to traverse new terrain. The costs occasioned by the application to amend should be capped in terms of rule 32(11) and should be granted in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with the general rule that such costs are borne by a party who seeks an indulgence.

[36]	Both the third parties and the defendant indicated, during argument, that they are not liable jointly and severally for costs and that each one should cover only a portion of the costs arising from the opposed application for amendment. I agree. The plaintiff’s costs relating to the hearing of the application for amendment, including the costs relating to heads of argument thereanent should be borne on a 50-50 basis by the third parties on the one hand and the defendant on the other. 

[37]	The costs relating to the pleadings in the respective applications for amendment are separate, because the applications were filed separately, under different interlocutory case numbers. Therefore, the defendant and the third parties must bear such costs, severally. However, the overall costs to be recovered, by the plaintiff must not exceed the cap in terms rule 32(11), in either case.

[38]	The costs in terms of rule 52(8) stand on a different footing and must be borne respectively by the third parties and the defendant.

[39]	Therefore, I make the following order:

Only the plaintiff opposes the applications.

[2]	The amendments sought seek to raise similar issues and the objections thereto to are in some material respects, also similar. Therefore, both applications were heard together on 17 June 2025, and it is convenient that both be disposed of in a single judgement. I shall proceed to do so.

[3]	The notice of intention to amend on behalf of the third parties was filed on 18 October 2024 and the one on behalf of the defendant was filed on 8 January 2025. The pleadings in the application brought by the third parties closed on 27 February 2025, whereas in the application brought by the defendant, such pleadings closed on 12 March 2025.

[4]	Both applications were initially set down for 16 May 2025, but could not be heard on that day, and the hearing was moved to 17 May 2025, for me to hear the matters, which I did, and upon which I reserved judgment, to be delivered on 8 July 2025.

[5]	I set out the above chronology, just to show that even an application to amend can delay a matter for more than six months and that care must be taken when amendments are initiated, and objections are taken to such amendments. In this matter, in view of the position I take, regarding the amendments, the plaintiff who amongst others, objects to the amendments on the basis that it is brought late in the proceedings and will delay the matter by reopening of the pleadings, is responsible for the further delay in the ultimate finalisation of the proceedings. In my view the amendments should have been conceded or agreed to because the objections taken, in each case, are without merit.

[6]	The amendment sought by the third parties, as I have said above, relates to the plea to the third-party notice which was filed by the defendants. In addition to correcting some typographical errors, the amendment seeks to introduce two additional defences, one aimed at impugning the power, authority, or ability of the defendant to bind the Joint Venture between the defendant and the third parties to the contract entered into between the defendant and the plaintiff, with the additional assertion that the said contract was in any event objectively impossible to perform for a miner at the place from which the copper ore had to be mined, as stipulated in the contract, being Outani Mine and was for this reason concluded as a result of a mistake, misunderstanding or iustus error, and the second seeking to challenge whether there was consensus between the defendant and the plaintiff regarding the quality of the copper ore which had to be delivered in terms of the said contract.

[7]	The allegations relating to the mistake, misunderstanding or iustus error pertain to the quality of the copper that could be obtained from Outani Mine, for delivery to the plaintiff. The agreement describes the commodity as raw copper with the origin as per certificate of origin to be Namibia, the fineness to be ore, and purity to be tested between five percent and 25 percent with the average of 15 percent copper concentrate. Monthly production as per the agreement had to be ‘5000MT’ per month with the average of plus or minus five percent and sizes had to be ‘19mm’.

[8]	The third parties assert as per the intended amendment that it was objectively impossible for any miner in Namibia to produce copper ore of the purity stipulated in the agreement and that the scenario and the facts on which such an agreement is based is so unlikely that the purported conclusion of the agreement cannot be explained other than that it was based on iustus error, vitiating consensus. Either both the plaintiff and the defendant were mistakenly of the view that it was possible to perform in terms of the agreement, but had they known the true position, they would not have concluded the agreement (thus, they were operating under a common mistake), or there was a unilateral mistake by one or both of them (in the case of both, the mistake would be mutual), the inference sought to be drawn being that the mistake, in either case, must have been caused by culpable conduct or statements of the other party.

[9]	The evidence to support the notion that it was impossible to produce the quality and quantity of the copper ore stipulated in the agreement is set out in various witness statements of the witnesses to be called by the defendant and the third parties, including the expert summary of Dr Harwood and Dr Dixon. It was submitted on behalf of the plaintiff that such evidence would have been objected to as being in conflict with the defendant’s pleadings.

[10]	The plaintiff objects to the proposed amendments by the third parties on the bases that the proposed amendments are sought belatedly, at the advanced stage of the proceedings without an explanation under oath for such lateness. The plaintiff maintains further that the proposed amendments constitute a substantial change of front which will require the plaintiff to revisit the matter from the pleadings stage as well as to amplify its witness statements, expert evidence and discovery. The third basis of the objection is that the evidence is not foreshadowed to support the plea in its intended amended form and lastly that the third parties have not acknowledged liability for costs. Since the objections are similar to those raised against the proposed amendment on behalf of the defendant, I propose to deal with both sets of objections at once, herein below. 

[11]	It is common cause that the defendant was jolted into action after the amendments sought to be made on behalf of the third parties were filed and the defendant’s proposed amendments are modelled on those of the third parties. The defendant, in the first instance seeks to introduce an amendment for the proper construction to be placed on the provisions of the agreement dealing with the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. The amendment seeks to state that the purity the copper ore would achieve would be between five percent and 25 percent, alternatively an average of 15 percent copper concentrate, once upgraded to copper ore concentrate and that this could be achieved from raw copper ore with the content of about two percent in the ore. 

[12]	In the event of the above not being sustained, and in the alternative, the proposal sought rectification of the agreement, to reflect the above position, but such an attempt at rectification was abandoned and nothing more needs to be said about it.

[13]	The next amendment sought, seeks to introduce a further alternative defence (in the event of the defendant failing to have the defence based on the plea as amended in the first instance sustained), that the agreement as it stands is vitiated by lack of consensus regarding the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff and that such dissensus was caused by a common fundamental mistake that such a quality of ore existed at the Outani Mine and could be delivered, whereas raw copper ore of such quality does not exist at that mine or anywhere else in Namibia and cannot be delivered.

[14]	The final amendment sought to be introduced is that the agreement is unenforceable for being initially impossible (from the inception) to perform, because the quality of copper ore contended by the plaintiff to be what was agreed, cannot be found at the Outani Mine or anywhere else in Namibia.

[15]	Once again the plaintiff objects to the proposed amendments on the bases that they are sought belatedly, at the advance stage of the proceedings after discovery has already been made, witness statements and expert evidence have been filed, and without an explanation under oath why the amendment is sought so late in the proceedings. 

[16]	The objection is also on the bases that the amendment sought will introduce a change of front at a very late stage of the proceedings, which will require the pleadings, witness statements and discovery to be revisited and that no evidence is foreshadowed that will support the defendant’s plea as amended, as per the proposal. It is also said that the amendment will introduce a version which is mutually exclusive to the defences already contained in the defendant’s plea. In this regard, the plaintiff refers to para 6 of the defendant’s plea as it stands, where the defendant admits the written terms of the agreement. According to the plaintiff, the proposed amendment seeks to contradict that admission and will require contradictory evidence, which is impermissible.

[17]	Finally, the objection is also based on failure to tender costs or failure to acknowledge liability for costs.

[18]	For the assertion that an explanation under oath was required due to the belated nature of the amendment sought, the suggestion appears to be that the notice of intention to amend should have been accompanied by an affidavit explaining why the amendment is sought at such a late stage. This objection was taken before the applications to amend, supported by founding affidavits, were filed and the plaintiff persisted in those objection in argument, despite such affidavits having been filed. The argument is not so much that the explanation so provided is inadequate, but that no explanation is provided for the lateness. 

[19]	Both in the objections and the affidavits resisting the amendments, reliance was placed on the decision in Municipal Council of Windhoek v Pioneerspark Dam Investment CC for the proposition that late amendments are subject to greater scrutiny than before because of their deleterious effect upon the administration of justice and that although it is not a prerequisite for an application under rule 52(4) to be accompanied by an affidavit for simple and formal applications, the application for more substantial amendments such as withdrawing an admission or a substantial change of front would need to be done on affidavit.

[20]	I do not understand the above judgment to require that the notice of intention to amend, in terms of rule 52(1) must be accompanied by an affidavit, where the amendment sought is substantial. The judgment refers to rule 52(4) which makes it plain that the affidavit (and thus the explanation under oath) is required at the stage when a party applies to court for an amendment, after an objection is noted against its notice of intention to amend.

[21]	In the present case, both proponents for amendment filed affidavits explaining why amendments are sought at this late stage. The third parties did not initially retain senior counsel, but when the plaintiff, on 29 July 2024 amended its claim by essentially almost doubling the amount claimed from N$52 057 078,89 to N$88 942 503,90, a need was identified to retain senior counsel. The senior counsel so retained studied the record and realised that a defence along the lines of the proposed amendment should be raised and advised accordingly.

[22]	As for the defendant, when the proposed amendment was filed on behalf of the third parties, it was realised that a similar defence should be taken by the defendant. The requirement in the contract relating to the quality of the copper ore to be delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff was already in dispute, as per the existing plea. I refer to paras four and six of the amended particulars of claim and paras two, four, six and nine of the defendant’s plea, as it stands.

[23]	Thus, the intended amendments, in my view, seek to amplify the existing dispute rather than to constitute a complete change of front, and the delay in filing the amendments was explained. I, accordingly, do not agree that there was no explanation under oath for the late amendment and that the proposed amendment by the defendant constitutes a complete change of front or that the third parties seek to introduce completely new defences to the claim. I reject all such bases for the opposition to the proposed amendments.

[24]	As for the objection that the amendment does not raise a triable issue, I also do not agree with the submissions on behalf of the plaintiff. The third parties’ approach in this regard is clearly founded on the record of the documents as they are in the matter, including what is said in the respective witness statements of the parties. If indeed it is established at the trial, - matter which I am not required to decide at this stage, - that performance in terms of the agreement was impossible from the inception because the raw ore quality stipulated in the agreement is impossible to obtain in Namibia - (as asserted on behalf of the third parties and the defendant), - this may well vitiate the agreement. That is a triable issue, for impossibility of performance, in some instances, excuses performance. There is already a version from an expert witnesses, Dr Dixon and Dr Hawood, that this is indeed the case.

[25]	I do not find the version sought to be raised by the third parties to be mere speculation. Even though they are not parties to the agreement, the bases for lack of consensus in initio, which they seek to raise, are from proper inferences to be drawn from what is contained in the agreement, coupled with the evidence of witnesses as contained in the witness statements, that such quality of copper ore cannot be mined in Namibia, except, perhaps, at the Tsumeb Mine. This may result in the court holding that the contract was impossible to perform from the inception. 

[26]	If both the plaintiff and the defendant believed at the time that such quality of ore could be mined at the Outani Mine, and both were mistaken, they were operating under a common mistake in regard to the subject matter of the agreement. This will be the case if the evidence of Dr Dixon holds sway with the court, except, perhaps in the instance that the court finds that the ore could be obtained from the Tsumeb Mine. The agreement indicates that the ore had to be picked up at the ‘Mine site’ but does not seem to define the ‘Mine site’. This and the implications it has for the parties will have to be cleared up by evidence, but my view remains that these are triable issues.

[27]	I also do not see anything mutually exclusive or destructive in the version now sought to be put up by the defendant and what is contained in para 6 of the existing plea. What is clear to me is that the plaintiff and the defendant are in dispute as to the proper construction to be placed on the terms of the agreement describing the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. That construction will be given by the trial court after hearing evidence and in so far as the plaintiff’s counsel urged me, to at this stage provide an interpretation of that part of the agreement, I decline such an invitation.

[28]	I do so because in the matter of Total Namibia (Pty) Ltd v OBM Engineering and Petroleum Distrubutors CC the Supreme Court, in providing an exposition of the new approach to interpretation, held that the context in which a document is drafted is relevant to its construction in all circumstances and that meaning of words is, to a significant extent, determined by the context in which they are uttered. The Supreme Court went on to hold that 

	‘[23] Again this approach seems to comport with our understanding of the construction of meaning, that context is an important determinant of meaning. It also makes plain that interpretation is 'essentially one unitary exercise' in which both text and context, and in the case of the construction of contracts, at least, the knowledge that the contracting parties had at the time the contract was concluded, are relevant to construing the contract. This unitary approach to interpretation should be followed in Namibia. A word of caution should be noted. In accepting that the distinction between 'background circumstances' and 'surrounding circumstances' should be abandoned, courts should remember that the construction of a contract remains, as Harms JA emphasised in the E KPMG case, 'a matter of law, and not of fact, and accordingly, interpretation is a matter for the court and not for witnesses'. 

[24] The approach adopted here requires a court engaged upon the construction of a contract to assess the meaning, grammar and syntax of the words used, as well as to construe those words within their immediate textual context, as well as against the broader purpose and character of the document itself. Reliance on the broader context will thus not only be resorted to when the meaning of the words viewed in a narrow manner appears ambiguous. Consideration of the background and context will be an important part of all contractual interpretation.’

[29]	It is accordingly clear to me that the proper construction to be placed on the disputed terms of the agreement is a matter for the trial court, to be done after evidence is heard on the surrounding circumstances, the context and the background.

[30]	The objection relating to costs occasioned by the amendment was taken, perhaps without proper application of the mind to the rules applicable to amendments. Rule 52(8) provides that a party giving notice of amendment is, unless the court otherwise orders, liable to pay the costs thereby occasioned to any other party. The plaintiff does not point to any direction to the contrary or why it is of the view that it will otherwise not be entitled to such costs.

[31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. The costs of the application to amend stand on a different footing. They are to be capped in terms of rule 32(11), unless otherwise ordered.

[32]	I also agree with the submission on behalf of all the parties that the court may grant an amendment at any stage of the proceedings, before judgment and also that amendments of pleadings should be allowed in order to obtain a proper ventilation of the dispute between the parties so that justice may be done.

[33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable. In my view, the amendments sought in the present matter should have been agreed to so as to facilitate progress in the proceedings, which have now been delayed for a period of more than six months. I can however not say that the opposition was unreasonable, considering the stage in the proceedings at which the amendments were sought.

[35]	Even though the pleadings, as sought to be amended, involve complex questions of law, the law relating to amendments is trite and I did not have to traverse new terrain. The costs occasioned by the application to amend should be capped in terms of rule 32(11) and should be granted in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with the general rule that such costs are borne by a party who seeks an indulgence.

[36]	Both the third parties and the defendant indicated, during argument, that they are not liable jointly and severally for costs and that each one should cover only a portion of the costs arising from the opposed application for amendment. I agree. The plaintiff’s costs relating to the hearing of the application for amendment, including the costs relating to heads of argument thereanent should be borne on a 50-50 basis by the third parties on the one hand and the defendant on the other. 

[37]	The costs relating to the pleadings in the respective applications for amendment are separate, because the applications were filed separately, under different interlocutory case numbers. Therefore, the defendant and the third parties must bear such costs, severally. However, the overall costs to be recovered, by the plaintiff must not exceed the cap in terms rule 32(11), in either case.

[38]	The costs in terms of rule 52(8) stand on a different footing and must be borne respectively by the third parties and the defendant.

[39]	Therefore, I make the following order:

This objection was taken before the applications to amend, supported by founding affidavits, were filed and the plaintiff persisted in those objection in argument, despite such affidavits having been filed. The argument is not so much that the explanation so provided is inadequate, but that no explanation is provided for the lateness. 

[19]	Both in the objections and the affidavits resisting the amendments, reliance was placed on the decision in Municipal Council of Windhoek v Pioneerspark Dam Investment CC for the proposition that late amendments are subject to greater scrutiny than before because of their deleterious effect upon the administration of justice and that although it is not a prerequisite for an application under rule 52(4) to be accompanied by an affidavit for simple and formal applications, the application for more substantial amendments such as withdrawing an admission or a substantial change of front would need to be done on affidavit.

[20]	I do not understand the above judgment to require that the notice of intention to amend, in terms of rule 52(1) must be accompanied by an affidavit, where the amendment sought is substantial. The judgment refers to rule 52(4) which makes it plain that the affidavit (and thus the explanation under oath) is required at the stage when a party applies to court for an amendment, after an objection is noted against its notice of intention to amend.

[21]	In the present case, both proponents for amendment filed affidavits explaining why amendments are sought at this late stage. The third parties did not initially retain senior counsel, but when the plaintiff, on 29 July 2024 amended its claim by essentially almost doubling the amount claimed from N$52 057 078,89 to N$88 942 503,90, a need was identified to retain senior counsel. The senior counsel so retained studied the record and realised that a defence along the lines of the proposed amendment should be raised and advised accordingly.

[22]	As for the defendant, when the proposed amendment was filed on behalf of the third parties, it was realised that a similar defence should be taken by the defendant. The requirement in the contract relating to the quality of the copper ore to be delivered by the defendant to the plaintiff was already in dispute, as per the existing plea. I refer to paras four and six of the amended particulars of claim and paras two, four, six and nine of the defendant’s plea, as it stands.

[23]	Thus, the intended amendments, in my view, seek to amplify the existing dispute rather than to constitute a complete change of front, and the delay in filing the amendments was explained. I, accordingly, do not agree that there was no explanation under oath for the late amendment and that the proposed amendment by the defendant constitutes a complete change of front or that the third parties seek to introduce completely new defences to the claim. I reject all such bases for the opposition to the proposed amendments.

[24]	As for the objection that the amendment does not raise a triable issue, I also do not agree with the submissions on behalf of the plaintiff. The third parties’ approach in this regard is clearly founded on the record of the documents as they are in the matter, including what is said in the respective witness statements of the parties. If indeed it is established at the trial, - matter which I am not required to decide at this stage, - that performance in terms of the agreement was impossible from the inception because the raw ore quality stipulated in the agreement is impossible to obtain in Namibia - (as asserted on behalf of the third parties and the defendant), - this may well vitiate the agreement. That is a triable issue, for impossibility of performance, in some instances, excuses performance. There is already a version from an expert witnesses, Dr Dixon and Dr Hawood, that this is indeed the case.

[25]	I do not find the version sought to be raised by the third parties to be mere speculation. Even though they are not parties to the agreement, the bases for lack of consensus in initio, which they seek to raise, are from proper inferences to be drawn from what is contained in the agreement, coupled with the evidence of witnesses as contained in the witness statements, that such quality of copper ore cannot be mined in Namibia, except, perhaps, at the Tsumeb Mine. This may result in the court holding that the contract was impossible to perform from the inception. 

[26]	If both the plaintiff and the defendant believed at the time that such quality of ore could be mined at the Outani Mine, and both were mistaken, they were operating under a common mistake in regard to the subject matter of the agreement. This will be the case if the evidence of Dr Dixon holds sway with the court, except, perhaps in the instance that the court finds that the ore could be obtained from the Tsumeb Mine. The agreement indicates that the ore had to be picked up at the ‘Mine site’ but does not seem to define the ‘Mine site’. This and the implications it has for the parties will have to be cleared up by evidence, but my view remains that these are triable issues.

[27]	I also do not see anything mutually exclusive or destructive in the version now sought to be put up by the defendant and what is contained in para 6 of the existing plea. What is clear to me is that the plaintiff and the defendant are in dispute as to the proper construction to be placed on the terms of the agreement describing the quality of the copper ore to be delivered to the plaintiff. That construction will be given by the trial court after hearing evidence and in so far as the plaintiff’s counsel urged me, to at this stage provide an interpretation of that part of the agreement, I decline such an invitation.

[28]	I do so because in the matter of Total Namibia (Pty) Ltd v OBM Engineering and Petroleum Distrubutors CC the Supreme Court, in providing an exposition of the new approach to interpretation, held that the context in which a document is drafted is relevant to its construction in all circumstances and that meaning of words is, to a significant extent, determined by the context in which they are uttered. The Supreme Court went on to hold that 

	‘[23] Again this approach seems to comport with our understanding of the construction of meaning, that context is an important determinant of meaning. It also makes plain that interpretation is 'essentially one unitary exercise' in which both text and context, and in the case of the construction of contracts, at least, the knowledge that the contracting parties had at the time the contract was concluded, are relevant to construing the contract. This unitary approach to interpretation should be followed in Namibia. A word of caution should be noted. In accepting that the distinction between 'background circumstances' and 'surrounding circumstances' should be abandoned, courts should remember that the construction of a contract remains, as Harms JA emphasised in the E KPMG case, 'a matter of law, and not of fact, and accordingly, interpretation is a matter for the court and not for witnesses'. 

[24] The approach adopted here requires a court engaged upon the construction of a contract to assess the meaning, grammar and syntax of the words used, as well as to construe those words within their immediate textual context, as well as against the broader purpose and character of the document itself. Reliance on the broader context will thus not only be resorted to when the meaning of the words viewed in a narrow manner appears ambiguous. Consideration of the background and context will be an important part of all contractual interpretation.’

[29]	It is accordingly clear to me that the proper construction to be placed on the disputed terms of the agreement is a matter for the trial court, to be done after evidence is heard on the surrounding circumstances, the context and the background.

[30]	The objection relating to costs occasioned by the amendment was taken, perhaps without proper application of the mind to the rules applicable to amendments. Rule 52(8) provides that a party giving notice of amendment is, unless the court otherwise orders, liable to pay the costs thereby occasioned to any other party. The plaintiff does not point to any direction to the contrary or why it is of the view that it will otherwise not be entitled to such costs.

[31]	I also agree with the submissions made on behalf of all the parties that such costs are not affected by the provisions of rule 32(11) and are not to be capped. The costs of the application to amend stand on a different footing. They are to be capped in terms of rule 32(11), unless otherwise ordered.

[32]	I also agree with the submission on behalf of all the parties that the court may grant an amendment at any stage of the proceedings, before judgment and also that amendments of pleadings should be allowed in order to obtain a proper ventilation of the dispute between the parties so that justice may be done.

[33]	In my view, both amendments sought should be granted as set out in the respective notices of intention to amend. 

[34]	It is well established that a party seeking an amendment craves an indulgence from the court and should ordinarily bear the costs of amendment, even if successful, unless the opposition was unreasonable. In my view, the amendments sought in the present matter should have been agreed to so as to facilitate progress in the proceedings, which have now been delayed for a period of more than six months. I can however not say that the opposition was unreasonable, considering the stage in the proceedings at which the amendments were sought.

[35]	Even though the pleadings, as sought to be amended, involve complex questions of law, the law relating to amendments is trite and I did not have to traverse new terrain. The costs occasioned by the application to amend should be capped in terms of rule 32(11) and should be granted in favour of the plaintiff in accordance with the general rule that such costs are borne by a party who seeks an indulgence.

[36]	Both the third parties and the defendant indicated, during argument, that they are not liable jointly and severally for costs and that each one should cover only a portion of the costs arising from the opposed application for amendment. I agree. The plaintiff’s costs relating to the hearing of the application for amendment, including the costs relating to heads of argument thereanent should be borne on a 50-50 basis by the third parties on the one hand and the defendant on the other. 

[37]	The costs relating to the pleadings in the respective applications for amendment are separate, because the applications were filed separately, under different interlocutory case numbers. Therefore, the defendant and the third parties must bear such costs, severally. However, the overall costs to be recovered, by the plaintiff must not exceed the cap in terms rule 32(11), in either case.

[38]	The costs in terms of rule 52(8) stand on a different footing and must be borne respectively by the third parties and the defendant.

[39]	Therefore, I make the following order:

1.	The third parties (the applicants in case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00017), are hereby granted leave to amend their plea dated 22 March 2024, as set out in their notice of intention to amend, filed on 18 October 2024, and must file their amended plea under case number HC-MD-CIV-ACT-2022/04737, no later than 18 July 2025.

2.	The defendant (the applicant in case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00138), is hereby granted leave to amend its amended plea dated 30 July 2024, as set out in its notice of intention to amend, filed on 8 January 2025, and must file the amended plea under case number HC-MD-CIV-ACT-2022/04737, no later than 18 July 2025.

3.	The third parties are ordered to pay 50 percent of the plaintiff’s costs of opposition in the application to amend, including costs relating to drawing of heads of argument and preparation together with all the costs relating to pleadings under case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00017, such costs to be capped to the amount of N$20 000, as provided in rule 32(11) of the rules of court.

4.	The defendant is ordered to pay 50 percent of the plaintiff’s costs of opposition in the application to amend, including costs relating to drawing of heads of argument and preparation together with all the costs relating to pleadings in case number INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00138, such costs to be capped to the amount of N$20 000, as provided in rule 32(11) of the rules of court.

5.	The third parties are further ordered to pay the costs occasioned by the notice to amend filed on 18 October 2024, on an uncapped basis, contemplated in rule 52(8).

6.	The defendant is further ordered to pay the costs occasioned by the notice to amend filed on 8 January 2025, on an uncapped basis, as contemplated in rule 52(8).

7.	The matters in case numbers INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00017 and INT-HC-AMDPLEA-2025/00138 are finalised and removed from the roll.

8.	The main matter under case number HC-MD-CIV-ACT-2022/04737 is postponed for a status hearing on 5 August 2025 at 15h00.

Reasons for order:

Ambunda J:

The Applicant approached this Court on an urgent basis seeking the orders as set out in the Notice of Motion filed of record and which appears on the e-justice system.  The Applicant is seeking interim relief with a return date and affording an opportunity to the Respondents to show cause why certain orders should not be made final on the return date.  The Applicants approaches this court on a truncated time periods as set out in the Notice of Motion, which indicates that should the Respondents wish to oppose the application, they must do so by 15 December 2025, that answering affidavits to be filed by 17 December and replying Affidavits to be filed by the 19th of December 2025, and that the return date should be the 22nd December 2025.  This is the same date as indicated in the Notice of Motion to be the return date for the rule nisi order sought.  

The second Respondent, cited in the papers, however opposed the matter just before it could be heard.  I must indicate that the matter was set down in terms of the Notice of Motion at 9 o’clock.  However, it could only be heard at 14h15 due to other urgent applications that were lined up as part of the Court’s business.  Therefore, by the time the matter was heard, there was opposition on the papers by the second Respondent.  

The 1st – 4th Applicants were represented by Mr Velikoshi and the second Respondent was represented by Adv Quickfall.  As preliminary factors, I have indicated to Counsel that only two issues needed to be addressed at this point. Firstly, in light of the fact that there is opposition by at least the second Respondent and secondly the issue on service.  I will start with the issue of service and summarise the facts at hand, as well as the arguments by the parties with respect to the issue of service.

Mr Velikoshi conceded that there are no returns of services filed of record and this is in respect of the first Respondent, being the master of the High Court, the second Respondent Mr Schickerling, the third Respondent, the Deputy Sheriff of Windhoek, the fourth Respondent, Mr Anguboyo and the fifth Respondent, being the Registrar of BIPA.  No returns of services has been filed off record as conceded to by Mr Velikoshi and addressed to the Court. Counsel also indicated that the documents have been dispatched to the deputy sheriff for service, but however no returns of services has been obtained. Counsel was in fact unsure whether service has been effected or not.  I say unsure because of the submission that Mr Velikoshi put on record, technically questioning how the second Respondent found himself before Court.  The court indicated to Counsel that, the fact that the second Respondent is in Court should be a blessing despite service not being done on him.  However, I need to put it on record that, that does not take away a party’s obligation to ensure that all parties are served before any Court order may be given and in fact, before a matter may be heard on anything.  The Court however, because of the presence of the second Respondent who, despite not being served, is before court, asked the parties to address the Court only on these two issues: service and urgency. 

Mr Velikoshi argued that the Court may dispense with the requirement for service, despite the parties not being served, despite the parties not being before Court, because in any event the order is only sought against the first and the second Respondent being the Master of the High Court and Mr Schickerling. Mr Velikoshi further made submission to the effect that despite the service, the urgency of the matter should guide the Court into still hearing the parties at least on the issue of urgency and that no prejudice will be done to the Respondents because of the nature of the order sought, being a form of a rule nisi with a return date, still gives the party an opportunity to come and place their cases before Court despite being served.

 Advocate Quickfall on the other end did not agree with this approach despite the fact that his client is in Court. It must be considered that the papers were not served on his client and that initially, he literally got instructions close to an hour before Court, indicating that the truncated time periods were not even enough to put together answering papers for purposes of the hearing.  In any event, Counsel further argued that service, despite this application not being brought as an Ex parte or where the requirement of service was not dispensed with, it is not one such application and the Court cannot waive the requirement for parties to be served.  

It is common cause from the papers that this is not an Ex Parte application and there are no circumstances that would render it necessary for a matter to be heard without service. The Applicant on its own papers does not even seek an order from the Court to condone a non-compliance with the rules of court, especially with regard to service. The next point that was then canvased by the parties and questioned by the Court is the non-appearance of the ordinary prayer in urgent applications to have the manner of service, the time periods within which to serve and notify other parties for purposes of proceedings to be truncated and to be condoned. That prayer is missing from the Applicant’s papers and as Adv Quickfall sets out, there is no basis on which this Court is even asked to condone non-service.  When the Court questioned Mr Velikoshi with regard to the absence of the prayer, Counsel was of the view that the Court may waive that requirement, alternatively incorporated in the further and/or alternative relief that is always sought at the end of every pleading filed with Court.  

The rules of Court and service are quite clear and as Rule 8 indicates how service should be done on persons, whether natural, artificial or corporate or company. The rules of Court are also very clear as to what instances service may be dispensed with especially when an application is brought as an Ex parte where circumstances would render it viable to not serve parties before an order is given.

A party is brought before Court by firstly notification and that notification has to be done through service in terms of the rules. If service is not done on a party, technically speaking, no order should be given and in fact this Court was not even obliged to hear the parties on anything until there are returns of services filed and that all parties are fully aware of the Court process and procedures, and the matter has been properly set down and for the parties to exercise their rights on whether to oppose or not.
