It does not take away the obligation of the parties to be served.  

There are exceptional circumstances under which service must be done and in this case the Applicants have not demonstrated any exceptional circumstances why this Court should waive service in these circumstances and for such an order to be granted in their favour. I also do not see any circumstances to justify an order to be made without service being done in all 4 Respondents.  That is beside the fact that the second Respondent is in Court.  

I have indicated at the beginning that ordinarily, this Court would not have heard the parties without proof of service.  Mr Velikoshi however indicated that despite non-service, the urgency of the matter justifies for the Court to hear the case and that service may be waived. Rule 73(4) is probably one of the most used rules in Court, so it is not alien to any of the parties.  The parties know exactly what the requirements for Rule 73 are. It indicates that in an affidavit in support of an urgent application, the party must explicitly and not mere lip service to the rule, set out the circumstances which he or she avers renders the matter urgent and the reason why he or she claims he or she could not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. From a careful reading of these paragraphs, they speak to the requirements of an interim interdict. I will briefly go through some of the factors that Counsel referred to as rendering this matter urgent.

I will demonstrate how. Furthermore, the second Respondent continues to act irresponsibly and in a manner that is not only bullish but also falls significantly short of the standard of conduct expected of a receiver and or liquidator occupying a position of judicially responsibility. Counsel also during his argument further pointed out that the conduct of the second Respondent specifically in removing assets and restricting the Applicant’s access to bank accounts has the effect of forcing the second Applicant into default of its financial obligations and causes it to seize its business operations.  These conducts are likely to result in the closure of business, loss of employment opportunities for its staff and the imposition of substantial penalties for breach of contractual commitments to its clients.  It was also mentioned of the fact that there is a Notice to Appeal to the Supreme Court which will be rendered futile if the conduct of the second Respondent is allowed to proceed.  

The court persistently asked Mr Velikoshi how the conduct of the first respondent constitute a ground for urgency and that question was asked in light of what the position in law is when it comes to alleged unlawful or ultra vires conduct of a person being used as a basis to approach the Court in an urgent basis. 

 I refer to the matter of Rosmund v Van Hil,l as well as the matter of Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd where the Court has indicated that the averments that the Respondents has acted illegally or will act illegally on their own does not constitute a ground of urgency.  Exceptional circumstances must be shown to exist before urgent relief is granted.  And the Court in the Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd matter said:

    ‘I am of the view that the fact that a litigant or Respondent in particular has embarked on an illegal crusade does not of its own render a matter urgent.  There must be something more than just illegality that warrants the invocation of urgency regime.  As it is, each matter must be pointed out, will turn on its own facts.  The view of the Court was that illegality of an action does not without more render the matter urgent.  There will be circumstances where an illegal action coupled with other considerations may render the matter urgent and there may be other circumstances where the same results does not eventuate to however equate illegality to urgency it is in my conceded view not a correct approach.’

Now, coming back to the facts of this case and having considered the type of conduct that is being complained of by the Applicants, in a nutshell, it can be summarised that the second respondent is seen to be on a frolic of his own and is acting in an unlawful or unwarranted manner.  From the authorities as indicated above, that alone does not constitute urgency.  Did the Applicants prove more circumstances than that?  I think not.  I say so for the following reasons: much has been stated that if this Court order is not granted today for example the Applicant’s business will come to a standstill, people need to be paid, and the second applicant will be defaulting and its payments in respect of the properties and that of his business need to continue. I fail to understand this line of argument because it does not indicate how the conduct of the second respondent contributes to these consequences or how a lack of an urgent order will halt the Applicants’ business, especially in the face of two Court orders of a provisional and final liquidation relating to the Applicants, which already halts the business of the Applicant.  In light of those two orders, it is already ‘not business as usual’.  So, the conduct of the second Respondent can never be imputed to the extent that it is being used as a ground for urgency to indicate that if the matter is not heard on an urgent basis, the Applicant’s business is crumbling.  

The second leg of Rule 73(4) requires of a party to indicate why substantial redress cannot be obtianed at a hearing in due course. From the exchange of the Court with Mr Velikoshi, it became clear that the approach or the focus is more that if the second Respondent is allowed to continue, there will not be much left to savage, that it would be difficult to get back the properties that may be purchased by bona fide purchasers. 

The requirement of Rule 73(4) must be properly understood.  It would mean that if this Court does not give the order today, that will be the end of it, and there is no other remedy that will be available to the Applicant in due course.  It is in that light that the Court needs a party to define and set out a reason why it indicates that it will not be afforded substantial redress at a hearing in due course. Clearly, in this matter and it is something that Adv Quickfall also touched on, there are mechanisms and remedies available, for example, to approach the Master of the High Court, to ask for the removal of a liquidator if the parties are of the opinion that a nominee or liquidator or receiver is not acting in accordance with their powers as given  in terms of the appointments by the Master.  So, there are remedies available to the Applicant, this is not the end of the matter.  

The Applicants have not made out a case where this Court should waive the requirement of service.  Secondly, the Applicants have not made out a case as to why this matter should be heard on an urgent basis.  These are all procedural aspects that have not been complied with, and the appropriate order would be to strike the matter from the roll for lack of urgency and service.  

With regard to costs, Mr Quickfall submitted that costs should be given on a punitive scale because the matter should not even be here.  I however refrain from giving a punitive scale because I do not have circumstances warranting any intentional or vexatious conduct on the part of the Applicant, save to have presented a case with procedural pitfalls.  So, costs will follow on a normal scale, such costs to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, in favour of second Respondent, who has at least thus far opposed the matter.  

The order of the Court is then as follows:

The application by the Applicant is struck from the roll for lack of urgency and lack of service on the respondents.  

Costs are awarded in favour of the second Respondent, such cost to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, and;

 The urgent application is removed from the roll and considered finalised.

I will demonstrate how.  The Applicants in paragraph 50 says, and this speaks to prima facie right in respect of the interim interdict relief, that the second Respondent acted without proper authority, has abused such authority, and has exceeded the scope of any authority he believed to possess or has otherwise improperly obtained such authority.  Accordingly, the second Respondent has acted with impunity to the detriment not only of the second Applicant but also third parties including the employees and banking institutions.  It is manifest that the second Respondent has demonstrated a disregard of a Court order and unless his conduct is interdicted, there is a real risk that he will continue to act with impunity.

The affidavit further sets out that the actions of the second Respondent, and this is from paragraph 51, in his capacity as both receiver and provisional liquidator are unlawful and constitutes a direct infringement of the Applicant’s rights as well as those of third parties.  Furthermore, the second Respondent continues to act irresponsibly and in a manner that is not only bullish but also falls significantly short of the standard of conduct expected of a receiver and or liquidator occupying a position of judicially responsibility. Counsel also during his argument further pointed out that the conduct of the second Respondent specifically in removing assets and restricting the Applicant’s access to bank accounts has the effect of forcing the second Applicant into default of its financial obligations and causes it to seize its business operations.  These conducts are likely to result in the closure of business, loss of employment opportunities for its staff and the imposition of substantial penalties for breach of contractual commitments to its clients.  It was also mentioned of the fact that there is a Notice to Appeal to the Supreme Court which will be rendered futile if the conduct of the second Respondent is allowed to proceed.  

The court persistently asked Mr Velikoshi how the conduct of the first respondent constitute a ground for urgency and that question was asked in light of what the position in law is when it comes to alleged unlawful or ultra vires conduct of a person being used as a basis to approach the Court in an urgent basis. 

 I refer to the matter of Rosmund v Van Hil,l as well as the matter of Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd where the Court has indicated that the averments that the Respondents has acted illegally or will act illegally on their own does not constitute a ground of urgency.  Exceptional circumstances must be shown to exist before urgent relief is granted.  And the Court in the Dr Tjipangandjara v Namibia Water Corporation (Pty) Ltd matter said:

    ‘I am of the view that the fact that a litigant or Respondent in particular has embarked on an illegal crusade does not of its own render a matter urgent. I fail to understand this line of argument because it does not indicate how the conduct of the second respondent contributes to these consequences or how a lack of an urgent order will halt the Applicants’ business, especially in the face of two Court orders of a provisional and final liquidation relating to the Applicants, which already halts the business of the Applicant.  In light of those two orders, it is already ‘not business as usual’.  So, the conduct of the second Respondent can never be imputed to the extent that it is being used as a ground for urgency to indicate that if the matter is not heard on an urgent basis, the Applicant’s business is crumbling.  

The second leg of Rule 73(4) requires of a party to indicate why substantial redress cannot be obtianed at a hearing in due course. From the exchange of the Court with Mr Velikoshi, it became clear that the approach or the focus is more that if the second Respondent is allowed to continue, there will not be much left to savage, that it would be difficult to get back the properties that may be purchased by bona fide purchasers. 

The requirement of Rule 73(4) must be properly understood.  It would mean that if this Court does not give the order today, that will be the end of it, and there is no other remedy that will be available to the Applicant in due course. With regard to costs, Mr Quickfall submitted that costs should be given on a punitive scale because the matter should not even be here.  I however refrain from giving a punitive scale because I do not have circumstances warranting any intentional or vexatious conduct on the part of the Applicant, save to have presented a case with procedural pitfalls. The application by the Applicant is struck from the roll for lack of urgency and lack of service on the respondents.  

Costs are awarded in favour of the second Respondent, such cost to include the cost of one instructing and one instructed Counsel, and;

 The urgent application is removed from the roll and considered finalised.

Reasons for orders:
PRINSLOO DJP:

Introduction

This is an application for leave to appeal against the court’s refusal to compel the respondent to discover documents. 

In the notice in terms of Rule 28(8)(a), the applicants sought further discovery of  documents in the following terms:

         ‘1. All documents that indicate exactly what discounts were received by the plaintiff when the defendant bought merchandise at authorised Shoprite Wholesalers or distributors.

2. All documents indicating how much of such discount, as envisaged in paragraph 1 above, was used by Shoprite on operational expenses.

3. All documents indicating how the amounts in paragraphs 1 and 2 above were treated in the plaintiff's annual financial statements.'

       Having heard the arguments, Miller AJ delivered a concise ruling on 26 November 2024 and made the following order: 

‘1. The application is dismissed.
2. The plaintiff is entitled to costs, which will be capped as provided for in Rule 32(11). 
3. The interlocutory is finalised and removed from the roll.’

The applicants aggrieved by the outcome of the application filed their application for leave to appeal, as the applicants are of the view that it is clear from the pleadings that the documents sought to be discovered are available. 

The parties

The applicants are as follows:

The first applicant is Amarula Investment CC, duly registered and incorporated in accordance with the applicable laws of Namibia, with principal place of business situated at Shop No. 1, Erf 3296, Maroela Mall, Mandume Ndemufayo Road, Ongwediva, Namibia. The first applicant was a franchisee of the respondent and operates a supermarket retail store. 

The second and third applicants are Gerome Meshawn Schmidt and Amalia Maxine Schmidt, residing in Ongwediwa.

The fourth applicant is Schmidtco. Property Development Company (Pty) Ltd, a private company with limited liability, duly incorporated in terms of the laws of the Republic of Namibia with its registered address at Erf No. 3507, Ongwediva, Namibia and at Shop No. 40, Erf 3296, Maroela Mall, Mandume Ndemufayo Road, Ongwediva. 

The respondent is Shoprite Namibia (Pty) Ltd, a private company with limited liability, duly incorporated and registered in accordance with the applicable laws of Namibia, doing business as a wholesale franchisor and central purchasing agency, with principal place of business situated at 32 Moses Tjitendero Street, Olympia, Windhoek, Namibia.

Background

In the main action, the plaintiff claims payment from the defendants in the sum of N$8 189 040, 82; N$6 051 438, 93; N$1 926 134, 77, together with ancillary relief.

The amounts claimed arise from a franchise agreement concluded between the parties in terms whereof, inter alia, the first defendant acquired the right to trade under the name and style of 'OK Foods'.

The business of the plaintiff as a central purchasing organisation entails, among other things, that the plaintiff purchases commodities in bulk from suppliers and manufacturers on behalf of its members. The plaintiff's members are general retail dealers, such as supermarkets like the first defendant, conducting business throughout Namibia. The retail dealers achieve membership from the plaintiff. A member's membership enables them to obtain favourable credit facilities for purchasing stock from suppliers through the plaintiff. The suppliers invoice the plaintiff directly for supplies provided to a member, and the plaintiff pays the suppliers directly. In return, the member pays the plaintiff. The plaintiff provides the member with a statement of account reflecting the amount due, which is payable within 30 days of the date of the statement. 

The first defendant allegedly failed to make payment in terms of the respective agreements between the parties.

Issues for determination

Two issues arise in the determination of this application. The first is whether the order is appealable. The second is whether an appeal would have reasonable prospects of success, even if the order were appealable.

Appealability of the order

 
The applicants argued that a refusal to compel discovery is appealable with leave under certain factual circumstances. In this case, the order refusing to compel discovery severely restricts and limits both the applicants’ defence and counterclaim. Without the requested documents, the applicants will not be able to demonstrate to the court how much the respondent benefited from rebates and discounts at the expense of the applicants. 

The applicants further aver that the court made an order on facts not pleaded and that the court erred in dismissing the application to compel. 

The respondent’s case is that the order that the applicant sought to appeal against is interlocutory in nature and is not appealable as none of the required attributes, consisting of a) the order must be final in effect and not susceptible to alteration by the court of first instance, b) it must be definitive of the rights of the parties, c) and it must have the effect of disposing at least a substantial portion of the relief claimed in the main proceedings, are present. 

Discussion

In Central Technical Supplies v Paragon Investment JV China Huayun Group,  Angula AJA (as he then was) stated as follows:

           ‘[31] The test of whether a judgment or order is appealable was laid down by this Court in Vaatz & others v Klotsch & others with reference and approval of Erasmus: Superior Court Practice where the learned author reviewed the South African jurisprudence and concluded that an appealable judgment or order has three attributes: namely that (i) the decision must be final in effect and not susceptible to alteration by the court of first instance; (ii) it must be definitive of the rights of the parties, ie it must grant definitive relief; and (iii) it must have the effect of disposing of at least a substantial portion of the relief claimed in the main proceedings.
[32] This Court in Shetu Trading v Tender Board of Namibia observed, with reference to the view expressed by the SCA, that the question of appealability is ‘intrinsically difficult’ and ‘a vexed issue’ and that the principles set out in Zweni v Minister of Law and Order are not ‘cast in stone’ but are illustrative, and ‘not immutable’. The court further pointed out that there are cases where courts have held that a judgment or order is appealable when one attribute is missing, while there are cases where the judgment or order is unappealable despite all three attributes being present.’
Applying the criteria to the current facts, I must agree with the respondent’s position that Miller AJ’s ruling does not possess any of the three attributes set out above.

In my view, all the applicants have to do, is file a Rule 28(8)(a) notice in which they specify the documents in such detail that there is certainty and the plaintiff is able to identify the documents. 

The notice seeking the specific discovery is overbroad. The applicants sought a smorgasbord of documents, but their notices lacked specificity. When seeking discovery, specificity is crucial. Discovery requests should clearly and precisely identify the information or documents sought. This includes specifying the items to be produced, either by individual item or category, and describing each with reasonable particularity. The respondent would only be able to properly respond to a notice in terms of rule 28(8) once properly specified.

Therefore, in my view, the ruling dated 26 November 2024 is not appealable and the leave sought stands to be struck from the roll.

Prospects of success

It is well established that there must be reasonable prospects of success on appeal, but given the circumstance of the matter, I am of view that the appeal in casu, would have no reasonable prospects of success as another court, more specifically the Supreme Court, would not take a different view and compel discovery on the current facts.

PRINSLOO DJP:

Introduction

This is an application for leave to appeal against the court’s refusal to compel the respondent to discover documents. 

In the notice in terms of Rule 28(8)(a), the applicants sought further discovery of  documents in the following terms:

         ‘1. All documents that indicate exactly what discounts were received by the plaintiff when the defendant bought merchandise at authorised Shoprite Wholesalers or distributors.

2. All documents indicating how much of such discount, as envisaged in paragraph 1 above, was used by Shoprite on operational expenses.

3. All documents indicating how the amounts in paragraphs 1 and 2 above were treated in the plaintiff's annual financial statements.'

       Having heard the arguments, Miller AJ delivered a concise ruling on 26 November 2024 and made the following order: 

‘1. The application is dismissed.
2. The plaintiff is entitled to costs, which will be capped as provided for in Rule 32(11). 
3. The interlocutory is finalised and removed from the roll.’

The applicants aggrieved by the outcome of the application filed their application for leave to appeal, as the applicants are of the view that it is clear from the pleadings that the documents sought to be discovered are available. 

The parties

The applicants are as follows:

The first applicant is Amarula Investment CC, duly registered and incorporated in accordance with the applicable laws of Namibia, with principal place of business situated at Shop No. 1, Erf 3296, Maroela Mall, Mandume Ndemufayo Road, Ongwediva, Namibia. The first applicant was a franchisee of the respondent and operates a supermarket retail store. 

The second and third applicants are Gerome Meshawn Schmidt and Amalia Maxine Schmidt, residing in Ongwediwa.

The fourth applicant is Schmidtco. Property Development Company (Pty) Ltd, a private company with limited liability, duly incorporated in terms of the laws of the Republic of Namibia with its registered address at Erf No. 3507, Ongwediva, Namibia and at Shop No. 40, Erf 3296, Maroela Mall, Mandume Ndemufayo Road, Ongwediva. 

The respondent is Shoprite Namibia (Pty) Ltd, a private company with limited liability, duly incorporated and registered in accordance with the applicable laws of Namibia, doing business as a wholesale franchisor and central purchasing agency, with principal place of business situated at 32 Moses Tjitendero Street, Olympia, Windhoek, Namibia.

Background

In the main action, the plaintiff claims payment from the defendants in the sum of N$8 189 040, 82; N$6 051 438, 93; N$1 926 134, 77, together with ancillary relief.

The amounts claimed arise from a franchise agreement concluded between the parties in terms whereof, inter alia, the first defendant acquired the right to trade under the name and style of 'OK Foods'.

The business of the plaintiff as a central purchasing organisation entails, among other things, that the plaintiff purchases commodities in bulk from suppliers and manufacturers on behalf of its members. The plaintiff's members are general retail dealers, such as supermarkets like the first defendant, conducting business throughout Namibia. The retail dealers achieve membership from the plaintiff. A member's membership enables them to obtain favourable credit facilities for purchasing stock from suppliers through the plaintiff. The suppliers invoice the plaintiff directly for supplies provided to a member, and the plaintiff pays the suppliers directly. In return, the member pays the plaintiff. The plaintiff provides the member with a statement of account reflecting the amount due, which is payable within 30 days of the date of the statement. 

The first defendant allegedly failed to make payment in terms of the respective agreements between the parties.

Issues for determination

Two issues arise in the determination of this application. The first is whether the order is appealable. The second is whether an appeal would have reasonable prospects of success, even if the order were appealable.

Appealability of the order

 
The applicants argued that a refusal to compel discovery is appealable with leave under certain factual circumstances. In this case, the order refusing to compel discovery severely restricts and limits both the applicants’ defence and counterclaim. Without the requested documents, the applicants will not be able to demonstrate to the court how much the respondent benefited from rebates and discounts at the expense of the applicants. 

The applicants further aver that the court made an order on facts not pleaded and that the court erred in dismissing the application to compel. 

The respondent’s case is that the order that the applicant sought to appeal against is interlocutory in nature and is not appealable as none of the required attributes, consisting of a) the order must be final in effect and not susceptible to alteration by the court of first instance, b) it must be definitive of the rights of the parties, c) and it must have the effect of disposing at least a substantial portion of the relief claimed in the main proceedings, are present. 

Discussion

In Central Technical Supplies v Paragon Investment JV China Huayun Group,  Angula AJA (as he then was) stated as follows:

           ‘[31] The test of whether a judgment or order is appealable was laid down by this Court in Vaatz & others v Klotsch & others with reference and approval of Erasmus: Superior Court Practice where the learned author reviewed the South African jurisprudence and concluded that an appealable judgment or order has three attributes: namely that (i) the decision must be final in effect and not susceptible to alteration by the court of first instance; (ii) it must be definitive of the rights of the parties, ie it must grant definitive relief; and (iii) it must have the effect of disposing of at least a substantial portion of the relief claimed in the main proceedings.
[32] This Court in Shetu Trading v Tender Board of Namibia observed, with reference to the view expressed by the SCA, that the question of appealability is ‘intrinsically difficult’ and ‘a vexed issue’ and that the principles set out in Zweni v Minister of Law and Order are not ‘cast in stone’ but are illustrative, and ‘not immutable’. The court further pointed out that there are cases where courts have held that a judgment or order is appealable when one attribute is missing, while there are cases where the judgment or order is unappealable despite all three attributes being present.’
Applying the criteria to the current facts, I must agree with the respondent’s position that Miller AJ’s ruling does not possess any of the three attributes set out above.

In my view, all the applicants have to do, is file a Rule 28(8)(a) notice in which they specify the documents in such detail that there is certainty and the plaintiff is able to identify the documents. 

The notice seeking the specific discovery is overbroad. The applicants sought a smorgasbord of documents, but their notices lacked specificity. When seeking discovery, specificity is crucial. Discovery requests should clearly and precisely identify the information or documents sought. This includes specifying the items to be produced, either by individual item or category, and describing each with reasonable particularity. The respondent would only be able to properly respond to a notice in terms of rule 28(8) once properly specified.

Therefore, in my view, the ruling dated 26 November 2024 is not appealable and the leave sought stands to be struck from the roll.

Prospects of success

It is well established that there must be reasonable prospects of success on appeal, but given the circumstance of the matter, I am of view that the appeal in casu, would have no reasonable prospects of success as another court, more specifically the Supreme Court, would not take a different view and compel discovery on the current facts. 

Costs

The costs must follow the result. Costs are thus, awarded to the respondent. Such costs to include the costs of one instructing and one instructed counsel. The costs are limited to rule 32(11). 

My order is set out above.
